sentences.text: Dasornis was a massive bird with a wingspan that exceeded 5 meters and may have reached 6 meters.
The complete head and bill of this creature measured almost 45 centimeters in life.
Its eye socket had a diameter of 55 millimeters, while the distal end of the humerus was about 35 millimeters wide.
The first fossil of Dasornis emuinus, a right humerus shaft, was found in the Isle of Sheppey and misidentified as a paleognath bone by James Scott Bowerbank in 1854.
Richard Owen established the genus Dasornis in 1870 based on a broken skull found in the same deposits as the first specimen.
A well-preserved skull lacking the beak was discovered in the Isle of Sheppey London Clay at the start of the 21st century.
There are 24 recorded fossil occurrences of Dasornis in the Paleobiology Database.
Dasornis belongs to the parent group Pelagornithidae.
The genus is classified within the family Pelagornithidae.
Dasornis is classified in the order Odontopterygiformes due to uncertainty regarding its closest relatives.
The current valid name Dasornis emuinus combines the oldest valid genus and species names used for these fossils.
The genus Dasornis includes several junior synonyms such as Argillornis, Dasyornis, Megalornis, and Neptuniavis.
The species Dasornis emuinus has numerous junior synonyms including Argillornis emuinus, Megalornis emuinus, and Odontopteryx.
Most Dasornis fossils date to approximately 50 million years ago and were found in the Early Eocene London Clay of the Isle of Sheppey in England.
A few tentatively assigned Dasornis remains from approximately 45 million years ago were found in the Middle Eocene of Etterbeek, Belgium.
Dasornis lived from the Selandian to the Priabonian stages, between 61.66 and 33.9 million years ago.
It is debated whether Dasornis was restricted to the North Atlantic and Paratethys or also occurred in the Pacific and Southern Hemisphere.
